reviews.review_title: Extremely light weight, great feel, comfortable to use.
reviews.review_description:
The first thing you notice about this mouse is the weight; it feels like a feather. This is also my first-ever Yunzii mouse. I’ve used many of their keyboards, so this had my attention immediately.

I am first always looking at the packaging of a product. I realize nice products can be packed in simple boxes, but I like a well-packed product. It comes in a very sturdy box with an outer sleeve. Inside the box is spongy foam to protect the mouse. Included in the box are stick-on fabric-like stickers to help with grip. The exterior is described as “carbon fiber texture” with a matte finish. I wasn’t loving the look in the beginning, but after using this, I am sold. That texture feels so good and really helps me with holding the mouse easily. I don’t feel the sticker grips are really needed for my use.

I use a corded mouse, but I am really liking the cordless aspect. You can use this Bluetooth, WiFi, or wired. The accompanying USB-A to USB-C cord is a braided cord (another detail I have grown to love). I do wish the cord was a bit longer; it works with my set up, but someone else’s setup may not have enough to connect. Yes, you can use it wireless, but take note in the description of how each connection rates with responsiveness.

The USB dongle to connect WiFi comes concealed in the mouse, which I stumbled upon when removing the stickers on the bottom. I had some difficulty getting this BT connected to my PC, not sure what exactly was happening, but I finally found it and worked great. It connected with no problem to my Mac computer with BT. It does have lightning-fast movement, which you can adjust by pushing the DPS button on the bottom. Along with the two top buttons and scrolling wheel, there are two side buttons. Features can be customized on the Yunzii website. Just a note, this has no RGB lighting.

I like this mouse, especially the carbon fiber texture, but my only negative is the buttons click so loud. I would get used to it the more I use it, but in a quiet room, it can be a bit much. But that is just my preference; it’s not anything against the product. I would in the future look at more peripherals from Yunzii beyond keyboards alone.

Read more

I have several Yunzii mice, the C1, M1 and now the M2. Of the three, the M2 is my favorite. The M2 is larger than the C1 which is too small for me since I use a paw/claw grip for my mouse. It is very lightweight and highly responsive. I like to run my mouse wired to get the full polling rate consistently. Unfortunately, I don't love the cord that comes with this mouse for running it wired. It's very stiff and kinked from being folded in the package. So it creates quite a lot of drag. I'm using a cord from another mouse that's fabric braided and very soft. It lays smooth and doesn't create drag. One of the things that I like most about this mouse is the carbon fiber texture. It has a really nice nonslip feel. The mouse comes with grip tape that works very well also for a solid grip and gives the mouse a sporty look. I mostly use my mouse for gaming and I will say that the sensor is excellent with no lag so far. I will note that the scroll wheel does not have the free scroll option and there is no rapid fire button or RGB backlighting. Overall, this mouse offers excellent performance for a value price. While it doesn't have some features like free scroll or RGB lighting, the texture and included grip tape give it unique look and feel. I ordered the pink color because it fits the vibe of my gaming room and it's hard to find a pale pink mouse. I would definitely recommend this mouse as a decent entry level to mid range mouse for gaming.

reviews.review_title: Great lightweight mouse with a premium look
reviews.review_description:
I picked up the YUNZII M2 in white with the carbon-fiber-style pattern, and I’m really impressed with how good this mouse looks in person. The finish gives it a unique appearance without being overly flashy, and the white color looks especially clean on a desk setup.

At 63g, it’s also very lightweight without feeling like a cheap or flimsy mouse. The shape feels comfortable in the hand, and the overall construction seems very well put together.

I really like the flexibility of the connectivity options. It supports 2.4GHz wireless, Bluetooth, and wired USB-C, so you can use it pretty much anywhere. The USB-C port is also a nice touch, and the included wireless receiver can be stored inside the mouse when you’re not using it, which makes it much harder to lose.

The PAW3395 sensor and 30,000 DPI capability are impressive specifications for a mouse in this price range, and the included 8K wireless receiver is another nice feature for anyone who wants high polling rates for gaming.

The included braided USB-C cable is also a nice addition and matches the mouse well.

Overall, this feels like a mouse that gives you a lot of the features you normally have to pay considerably more for. The lightweight design, clean appearance, multiple connection options, USB-C charging, PAW3395 sensor, and 8K wireless capability make the YUNZII M2 a very attractive option.

**Pros:**

* Lightweight 63g design

* Great-looking white/carbon-fiber-style finish

* PAW3395 sensor

* Up to 30,000 DPI

* 8K wireless receiver

* 2.4GHz, Bluetooth, and wired connectivity

* USB-C

* Receiver storage inside the mouse

* Braided charging cable included

For the price, this is a really impressive package. If you’re looking for a lightweight wireless gaming mouse without spending a fortune, the YUNZII M2 is definitely worth considering.

Read more

I’m really impressed with this gaming mouse. The pink color is accurate to the pictures, and the carbon fiber decorative pattern is a nice touch that gives the mouse a little more personality without being over the top. It has a sleek, modern look and feels great in hand.

The responsiveness is excellent, with smooth and precise tracking that makes it great for both gaming and everyday use. I also really like how lightweight it is at just 63g, making it easy to move around without feeling bulky or tiring during longer sessions. The wireless options are convenient, and having customization through the software and web interface is a great bonus.

Overall, this is a great combination of performance, design, and functionality. Definitely a 5-star mouse for anyone looking for something lightweight, responsive, and stylish.

I really love this mouse. It is lightweight, incredibly responsive, and honestly feels even more responsive than my Razer Viper. The 8K Dongle is a nice addition too. You can plug it directly into the port by itself, or use the cable and extension that comes with it if you want to use the 8K feature that way.

The Carbon Fiber design might actually be my favorite part. It is such a pretty mouse and its uniqueness stands out from its competitors and their solid colors. I also like that you can change the DPI setting right on the bottom of the mouse.

Overall, it is simple, very light, and ultra responsive. Add in the really nice design and the price, and I think this mouse is absolutely worth it.

The YUNZII M2 is a fantastic lightweight gaming mouse that feels quick and responsive without sacrificing comfort. At only 63g, it’s easy to move around during long gaming sessions, and the PAW3395 sensor provides smooth, accurate tracking with plenty of DPI adjustment options. The tri-mode connectivity is extremely convenient, allowing me to switch between wired, Bluetooth, and 2.4GHz wireless depending on what I’m using it for. I also like the carbon-fiber-style finish and the ability to customize settings through the software or web interface. Overall, this is an excellent mouse for gaming and everyday use, especially for anyone looking for a lightweight wireless option with high-end features.

reviews.review_title: Great Clicks and Comfortable to Use
reviews.review_description:
This wireless mouse feels really nice in the hand. The shape is ergonomic, and I like the texture and overall feel while using it. It also comes with a cable and adapter, and I like having the option to connect either through the cable or Bluetooth.

My favorite part is definitely the buttons. Every click feels crisp and clean, with that satisfying clicking sound Yunzii does so well. I also have a Yunzii keyboard and really like the feel of both.

The mouse is very lightweight, which some people may prefer, but I personally like a little more weight and wish it felt slightly heavier. Other than that, it has been great for gaming with no noticeable latency.
This is a great quality Carbon fiber mouse 10/10 would reccomend very fast 8k polling and adjustable DPI

title: Razer Naga V3 Pro Wireless MMO Gaming Mouse with Swappable Side Plates
description:
Adapt and Unleash
Stay ahead of the game even when it changes. The Razer Naga V3 Pro is a modular wireless gaming mouse built to adapt across genres. Designed for MMO, battle royale, FPS, MOBA, RPG, and productivity use, it combines three swappable side plates with next-generation wireless performance, advanced scrolling technology, and precision tracking to deliver exceptional versatility. Command more, react faster, and customize your gameplay like never before.

Swappable Side Plates & Quick-Access Edge Buttons
Adapt your controls to match the game. Swap between 12-button, 6-button, and 2-button magnetic side plates to create the ideal layout for every genre. Access up to 23 programmable buttons, including two quick-access edge buttons for on-the-fly DPI adjustments and a lockable ring finger button that provides additional control when you need it most. Whether managing MMO skill rotations, assigning FPS utility commands, or streamlining productivity workflows, every action is within reach.

Razer HyperScroll Tilt Wheel Gen-2
Experience precise control and effortless navigation with the next generation of Razer scrolling technology. Choose between two tactile scrolling modes with 24 or 48 steps, switch to free-spin mode for rapid navigation, or enable Smart-Reel mode to automatically transition between tactile and free-spin scrolling based on scroll speed. With four-direction tilt inputs and customization through Razer Synapse, the wheel delivers greater flexibility for gaming and productivity.

Razer Optical Mouse Switches Gen-4
Built for speed, durability, and responsiveness. These optical switches deliver crisp tactile feedback, 12% lighter actuation, and a click lifecycle rated for over 100 million clicks. Enjoy fast, consistent execution for MMO ability rotations, rapid-fire commands in competitive shooters, and years of dependable performance.

Razer Focus Pro 50K Optical Sensor Gen-3
Track with confidence using Razer's most advanced sensor technology. Featuring up to 50,000 DPI, 930 IPS tracking speed, and 90G acceleration, the sensor is enhanced by Frame Sync technology for reduced latency and highly accurate cursor movement. From precision aiming in FPS titles to detailed cursor control during creative work, every movement is tracked with exceptional accuracy.

Multiple Connectivity Options for Every Situation
Choose the connection mode that best fits your setup. Razer HyperSpeed Wireless delivers ultra-low-latency performance for competitive gaming, Bluetooth provides extended battery life for everyday use, and USB Type-C wired connectivity enables charging and uninterrupted gameplay. With up to 155 hours of battery life on HyperSpeed Wireless and up to 280 hours on Bluetooth, the Naga V3 Pro is built to keep up with extended gaming sessions.

AI Prompt Master and Advanced Macros
Gain smarter control through AI-powered tools and advanced macro customization. Surface tailored gaming strategies faster with AI Prompt Master and execute complex chains of actions instantly with custom macros through Razer Synapse. Whether gaming, creating content, or managing productivity shortcuts, you'll have more ways to work and play efficiently.

reviews.review_title: I loved my Logitech. This is a viable replacement!
reviews.review_description:
I am a user, and fond lover, of the G502 and G600. When I saw V3 Pro and the feature set, I really wanted to take a dive into the Razer ecosystem and give it a whirl. This one mouse had the features and potential to replace both the G600 and G502 on my desk.

While using and trying the mouse, I can say that it does replace both and works as expected. The form may cause other pause, but it comes down to preference and usability. The G502 is a great mouse but was causing wrist issues despite the perfect for. The Naga V3 Pro is slightly smaller than the V2, but it has given me the form of the G600 which tends to be usable longer for me, with the features of the G600 and G502.

reviews.review_title: I don't like Razer, but this mouse slaps
reviews.review_description:
I was really, really contemplating rating this less because of Razer Synapse 4. I couldn't get button remapping to work in any game at the start, it would only work after I closed Synapse entirely. Profile switching also didn't work. The software took so much finagling and trial and error manually deleting Synapse and re-installing more than once--I even tried deleting Synapse data online from my account via the Privacy Center to no avail. Midway through, I almost just resorted to keeping things on onboard memory and manually switching between games. It was brutal.

Thankfully profile switching started working and button remaps followed suit. I don't know how I got it to work, but it works! It handles so well that the pain setting up the software can be forgiven. This is everything I wanted out of my old Logitech G600s, of which I've had several and daily drove for the better part of a decade. I'd always try but ultimately return other MMO mice because I'd always miss ring-finger button. I know I'm not the only one that felt this!

It seems like Razer heard our cries and implemented it on this new Naga V3 Pro, even adding the two additional buttons by the left-click button like on the V2 Hyperspeed. My only gripes are that the side buttons aren't as pronounced and contoured as the G600, and the left- and right-mouse clicks are just obnoxiously loud. Travel distance and weight per click as well I'd say aren't great either--maybe better for older MMOs where each click needed to be more deliberate, but a lighter switch would be better for modern MMOs. I guess I'll get used to them.

Despite all of that, the fact that in addition to the extra buttons this is wireless AND I can swap plates for other non-MMO games? I can learn to live with this.

Logitech really missed out.

Read more

I’ve been really impressed with the Razer Naga V3 Pro. My favorite feature is the removable side panels—it’s great being able to switch the button layout depending on what I’m doing. The mouse feels very solid and well-built, and the weight is just right for me. It feels comfortable and controlled without being too light.

My only issue has been the 2.4 GHz wireless connection. I haven’t been able to get it to run as smoothly as I’d like, so I normally toggle it over to Bluetooth, which has worked much better for me. Other than that, it’s a solid mouse and I really enjoy using it. Definitely one of my favorite mice I’ve owned.

Works great with 2, 6, or 12 side buttons. Razer Synapse customizes it with up to twice as many functions. Button on ring finger rest acts as trigger for second set on all Razer devices. Replaced my V2 with it.

reviews.review_title: Advanced features through Synapse Not supported in MAC
reviews.review_description: Synapse 4 currently does not support Razer Naga V3 Pro for MAC. This is ridiculous, and should be specified for buyers.

reviews.review_title: Good mouse design but questionable quality
reviews.review_description:
The buttons on the 12 button MMO panel wobble and creak. They are not sturdy. The buttons on the bottom right of the panel are impossible to use without fat fingering an extra key.

I like the scroll wheel and the third click. The scroll wheel is three extra buttons on its own. The third click should probably be used infrequently as it is an unnatural hand gesture.

I’m coming from an old razer naga x with keys that don’t jiggle, more solid construction, all for a lower price. Doesn’t seem like there’s an equivalent to it these days. I wish they would make another dedicated 12 button and stop giving the mmo players this junk three panel nonsense.
Top notch. Does about everything correct. Great feel, light, responsive, easy to customize. Lots of options.

Side buttons are too close to reasonable expect to select the correct one every time. Only one side panel is RGB. Mouse is too bulbous for smaller hands. Packaging is nonsense.

The HyperShift ring finger button is the only nice thing about the mouse. Or you'd think so.... Actually using it caused serious hand cramps during gaming. Retuned after 6 hours of use- back to the Basilisk

description:

reviews.review_title: The Ultimate Ambidextrous Endgame! 45 Days of Heavy Gaming and Pure Perfection
reviews.review_description:
I am coming back to write this review after putting this mouse through its paces for a solid 45 days. After upgrading my desktop with a premium 8K magnetic keyboard, I knew my mouse setup had to match that elite level of performance. That is why I pulled the trigger on the latest Razer Viper V4 Pro, and after a month and a half of intense daily use, it has completely redefined my gaming experience. If you are looking for the absolute pinnacle of symmetrical gaming mice, this is the endgame.

First, let us talk about the design because there is a lot of confusion out there. This Viper V4 Pro is a flawless, perfectly symmetrical shape. It is a completely different beast compared to the older, bulky, asymmetrical right-handed design of the DeathAdder V4 Pro. As someone who prefers a claw/fingertip grip for high-precision micro-adjustments, this symmetrical shell melts into my hand perfectly, giving my thumb and fingers ultimate control.

At a mind-blowing 49 grams, the weight distribution is pure wizardry. Combined with the native 8000Hz polling rate and the 50K DPI sensor, the tracking feels like an extension of my own nervous system. In high-APM gaming sessions and chaotic shooters like World War Z or CS2, swapping targets is instantaneous with zero initial drag. Furthermore, it is an absolute dream for massive open-world action games like Where Winds Meet. During high-stakes martial arts combat, dodging, executing flawless parries, and rapidly controlling the 3D camera feels incredibly smooth and responsive. There is absolutely no pixel-skipping or camera stutter, giving me perfect situational awareness.

Out of the box and after 45 days of absolute abuse, the build quality feels incredibly solid despite being so incredibly light—no creaking, no flexing, and the Gen-4 optical switches offer a crisp, satisfyingly tactical click that hasn't degraded a bit.

If I have to nitpick, running this monster at a full, unrestricted native 8K polling rate does drain the battery significantly faster than standard mice. It is a trade-off for infinite performance. However, the real sweet spot here is the 4K polling rate mode. With about 3 to 4 hours of gaming per day on the 4K setting, the mouse can easily coast for 8 to 10 days straight without even completely draining the battery to zero. This exceptional power efficiency completely eliminates any battery anxiety. Also, the premium price tag might make your wallet sweat, but for a top-tier esports weapon, you absolutely get what you pay for.

To sum it all up, the Viper V4 Pro is the undisputed king of symmetrical lightweight mice. It delivers unrivaled performance, unparalleled speed, and an incredibly locked-in grip. It has officially earned a permanent spot as the perfect crown jewel for my high-end setup. Highly recommended! Money well spent!

Read more

reviews.review_title: This is just one of my favorite mice now
reviews.review_description:
TLDR: This is the mouse I keep coming back to. Long story short, I want nothing more when using this mouse.

I'm one of those that just collects mice. I have my favorites, and I have some that I have just used once and put away. This is one that I keep bringing out. Simply put, the latest Viper and Deathadder are just some of my favorite mice period. They are built very solid, light weight, and flawless sensors. They have an instant wake up, fantastic battery life, satisfying clicks, great scroll wheel, and great side buttons. They are pricey, but quality-wise, it really doesn't get better than Razer now. And I'm comparing to Zowie, Logitech, G-wolves, Finalmouse, Pulsar, etc etc... Every one of those other brands has something I don't like in the quality alone, a creak, spongy click, or something keeps me from wanting to use those brands since I've used the Viper. Obviously, the shape is subjective, so if you've used the Viper V3 and didn't like the shape, you're not gonna like this. But I love the size shape, and weight. I can't wait to see the next Deathadder shed some weight to around 49g, and maybe implement some analog switches like the Logitech Superstrike. If they ever did that, I just hope they do weight balancing better because the superstrike is pretty front heavy, but I'm perfectly happy with Razer's optical switches because they just feel sooooo good. But I think the haptic analog switches would be very interesting in the Deathadder shape. I really don't know how they could improve on this other than finding more ways to lighten the weight even more. Razer might've perfected the Viper with this iteration.

Read more

This is the best gaming mouse as someone who upgraded from a regular stock mouse. The weight, the functionality, and the design of the mouse is perfect. In fact, this mouse, and it features had further fine-tuned my already decent aim. After using this mouse for a while, I have observed my aim became a natural aim bot, where I was even accused of potentially exploiting in a match of BF1.

The mouse itself is light, and as someone who came from a heavier mouse it felt a bit weird at first. However, if you can manage it, then it becomes a benefit. It allows you to flick quickly, and track targets consistently, which is where my claim of "natural aim bot" came from. It's not too light where you might find yourself tensing up too much to keep it in place, but if you came from a heavier mouse, then you might overflick your target a few times.

The features the mouse offered through Razer's Synapse software such as the DPI and mappings are very useful. You can set different profiles for different games, so there are different DPI's for each game. In addition, you can change the mouse's buttons to be mapped to keys on your keyboard. For example, you can have the side button mapped to 'R', so you can reload through the side button. You can also have the same side buttons run a macro, so if you're playing Helldivers 2, you can instantly input a stratagem through your side button. There are also features like letting the side buttons launch a program.

The mouse also features polling rates up to 8k, where higher rates increases the consistency of your cursor's tracking across the screen, and decreases latency. HOWEVER, higher rates can drain the battery life faster, and require specific hardware. Increased polling rates will put higher loads onto your CPU, so ensure you have a strong enough CPU. Otherwise, CPU intensive games will suffer FPS drops, or in general, some games might have issues or do not even support said polling rates. In addition, to notice the different in polling rates, a monitor with a higher refresh rate will be required. Regardless, using 2k and 4k, I haven't really noticed a difference as someone who has a 180hz monitor. It feels the same as 1k polling rate, but if you have the hardware to support it, use it!

Regarding the battery life, it's very very good. I have used 2k and 4k polling rates for hours in a day, and the battery only goes down from 100% to like 96%. Whereas if you use 1k polling rate, then the battery doesn't even drain at all till the next day or two maybe (I charge it overnight once the day ends).

Upgrading from a wired mouse, and as someone who was a firm believer that wired mice was better, this mouse changed that. I found the wireless mode of this mouse more consistent, than my wired mouse, and offered more freedom in wrist/arm movement. Therefore, I was able to track better. Also, the latency was small on it, perhaps even better. However, you can use the USB cable and plug it into the mouse if you'd like to use it wired.

The design of the mouse is comfortable for those who use a claw grip. I typically have my palm touching the mouse, and my fingers in a claw like stance on it. I found no discomfort, and was able to consistently aim. As for other grips, I do not know.

If you're upgrading from a stock mouse, then this is worth the upgrade. However, please read other reviews, if you're upgrading from like Razer's Viper V3 Pro mouse, then it might not be worth the money. Since the V3 shares many similarities to the V4 with a few new features.

Overall, this might be one of the best mice on the market right now. This mouse ended up being the final piece in the puzzle for me towards perfect aim. Somehow, my peripherals were holding me back, where it is typically the opposite.

Read more

I don’t typically write reviews, but this mouse is hands down the best I’ve ever had the pleasure of using, so I feel like I must. The moment my hand gripped the mouse, I knew it was the one. The build quality is fantastic. Everything. From the clicks to the sensor, the scroll wheel and the side buttons. Everything is perfect. The coating on the mouse is high quality and the dongle that comes with it is nicely weighted so it doesn’t slip around on your desk. The stock skates are also wonderful and glide around on my Artisan Zero Soft so smoothly. The size and shape is perfect for my grip style (relaxed claw) so I can handle it comfortably. I recently just bought a GPX Superlight 2 as well as an X2 Crazylight Medium and neither felt quite right. So I decided to try this mouse and it did everything for me the other two couldn’t. Since I bought the Razer Viper V4 Pro, I’ve seen a massive improvement in my gameplay. And for that reason I can confidently justify the price of this product. 5 Stars. Genuinely amazing product across the board. Dare I say perfect. 👍 ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️

reviews.review_title: Left me Surprised in a Good Way
reviews.review_description:
This mouse took me by surprise.

Coming from the Basilisk V3 Pro, this one is just so lightweight that I almost mistook it for a toy. I seriously can't believe how light this is.

The battery life is phenomenal, and the controls are astoundingly tight. The buttons on my Basilisk always felt cheap and mushy, but every button on this Viper V4 Pro is snappy and solid.

Getting to the part people care about most, this is probably the most fluid mouse I've ever used. The 50K sensor is a marketing ploy, as I don't use anything over 6400DPI, but you can turn on the 8K polling with a high refresh rate monitor and you won't see any dragging of your cursor across your screen as you will with lower refresh rates, and the higher polling rate shows your mouse's location on the screen more times per second than traditional 1K polling rates. My eyes can see the difference, but only if I strain to see it.

I run the mouse at 1K polling rate for optimal battery life and because most games are using that rate the most effectively. It's a sweet spot.

So the reasons to get the mouse are simple: lightweight, long battery life, no skipping, truly ambidextrous.

The cons: no wireless charging, and no RGB. But those are apparent tradeoffs for that impossibly light 49 gram feel.

Read more

The Razer Viper V4 Pro is a flagship-level esports mouse that doubles down on performance rather than reinventing the formula. It features an ultra-lightweight ambidextrous design at around 49–50g, paired with Razer’s Focus Pro 50K optical sensor capable of 50,000 DPI, 930 IPS tracking, and 90G acceleration. It also introduces Gen-4 optical switches, improved wireless performance with an upgraded dongle, and up to 180 hours of battery life. On paper, it’s one of the most technically refined mice available fast, consistent, and clearly built for competitive play.

That said, if you already own the Razer Viper V3 Pro, there’s honestly no real reason to upgrade. The improvements here are incremental slightly better battery life, marginally upgraded switches, and small refinements that you’re not going to feel in-game. The V3 Pro is already insanely lightweight, responsive, and accurate, so the V4 Pro ends up feeling more like a spec bump than a meaningful evolution. Unless you’re chasing absolute top-end specs for the sake of it, you’re better off sticking with the V3 Pro. As a stand alone mouse, I give it 4 stars. As a "upgrade" to the previous generation I'd give it one star.

reviews.review_title: New main. Excellent mouse with a ridiculous battery life
reviews.review_description:
The box didn't have much protection, but it arrived in great condition. As for the mouse itself, it is amazing.

I won't talk much about shape because that's highly subjective (I'll just say it fits my hand size and grip style), but everything else is excellent: coating is smooth and grippy, very nice to the touch; main clicks are light and tactile, tho they could have a little less post travel; side buttons are well tensioned and positioned; the wheel might be the weakest aspect, because the scrolling feels a bit off, but it's totally functional; M3 click is very tactile; skates are smooth and fast; build quality is perfect, solid as a rock; performance is top tier, no complaints; and finally, the battery is absolutely insane. I have been using the mouse for 12 days at 1000hz (sometimes 8000, but only for a couple of Apex matches) and it has only gone down to 60%.

On top of all of that, Razer has finally made a web software. That means 2 things: 1) you don't have to deal with the bloatware that is Synapse (except for firmware updates); and 2) you can change your settings on Linux, which has been a game changer for me (I dual boot Windows 11 and Bazzite).

I think it is worth the price, but only if you don't have a Viper V3 Pro (or even a Viper V3 Pro SE). On paper, the V4 Pro has many improvements, but the only real upgrade that a player will notice is the battery life and the web software. I recommend it to people who have never owned a Viper V3 and want the latest technology and power efficiency. I can recommend it to those who just want to try the shape, but they might also want to take a look at the V3 Pro, since it is cheaper right now.

Read more

I have been using it a full week now, and I think it's worth all the praise. It's a safe shape that will work for everyone except if your hands are on the smaller side. Switches, side buttons, scroll wheel, and sensor all feel perfect. My honest favorite thing about this mouse is the battery life is otherworldly good compared to anything I have used. I likely won't have to charge it until about 5-6 weeks of moderate to heavy use at 1000Hz, which is huge when I need to charge my other mice practically after a weekend.

The first negative is the price is steep, especially when you could get the V3 Pro Se for like have the price. Two, the M1/M2 switches are on the loud side, but you won't notice them with headphones. You will annoy anyone around you though if they have to listen to you click. Three, the black version is a bit of an oil magnet, but the coating at least feels good. Might be worth using either Razer's provided grips or another brands for long-term use.

Overall, it's a very good mouse if it's within your price range, and your hands are moderately large in size. Maybe it's placebo, but I also dropped my first nuke in Call of Duty on keyboard and mouse using it. That might be influencing might personal opinion of it, but I promise it's a great mouse.

title: Razer Viper V3 Pro Wireless Esports Gaming Mouse, 54g Lightweight, Black
description: The GOAT of wireless esports mice returns to reshape the competitive scene. Featuring a 54 g ultra-lightweight design and best-in-class technologies, the Razer Viper V3 Pro is the undisputed choice for peak performance and handling—the perfect weapon designed with and trusted by pros. reviews.review_title: my review of the razor viper v3 pro
reviews.review_description:
now for my background, i play r6 and csgo, and occasionally roblox shooters. i went from originally a 60g razer orochi v2 using a fingertip grip, and i went to this mouse with a traditional claw. i’ve had this mouse for a few months and i can say that this is a very good and universal shape for all sorts of grips. i have a medium size hand and i can comfortably fingertip and claw this mouse.

the coating is lovely and the best i’ve personally felt on a mouse, and i tried the grips but they eventually wear out over time so i don’t recommend using those (the actual mouse texture is better than the grips anyway). now i know this sounds a little ridiculous but moving from a 60g small mouse not even including the batteries, i played a LOT better with this bigger one after adjusting and i’m honestly happy with my purchase (even though it cost quite a bit). it feels light in the hand for the size and the weight is flawlessly distributed. the skates are solid for being stock but you can always upgrade, the scroll wheel is pretty normal and has distinctive bumps per scroll but personally i like more smoother ones (i am probably just being nitpicky). the main clicks are lovely to hear and the little dongle included doesn’t take up too much space, i’d say only the actual cable itself does but this isn’t actually an issue. the dongle can also support up to 8k hz which isn’t necessary but it’s a “nice to have” feature and i use 2k hz myself to save battery life;

speaking of battery life it’s pretty good and i suggest not using 8k since it drains it pretty fast but it lasts up to a week or two for me with regular use not charging (just remember to plug it in after use) the side buttons are a DEFINITE improvement from my old mouse and that was a perfect feature on the mouse. now, razer’s synapse software can be a little finicky sometimes but i suggest just configuring your settings and uninstalling it since it can take up some of your ram and overall performance.

in conclusion, this is a really good option for gaming mice and it can fit a LOT of playstyles. this has all of the latest mouse tech (might be a little outdated for me to be saying that in the big 25 now) and each part of the mouse is very pleasant to use. i suggest this mouse if you have the money (it is pretty ehh value for money but as long as you have the funds it’s a s tier mouse)

(Review from my 15 year old son)

Honestly this mouse felt SO much lighter than I thought it would. I just upgraded from the Glorious Model O- Wireless Gaming Mouse, and let me say... the upgrade was WORTH it for sure. I pretty much only play Fortnite on Keyboard and Mouse, and I was having issues with my side buttons on my old mouse. I decided it was time to upgrade since I can't have those issues happening mid-game. The Razer Viper V3 Pro, is definitely a solid upgrade. The side buttons are so much more solid than the side buttons on my old mouse. Not to mention, the response time of the clicks was faster, and the accuracy of my aim with the better sensor was so much better. The scroll wheel is also very responsive and fast which is important for Fortnite. (I was able to easily quad edit in Fortnite when using this new mouse)

The wireless connectivity isn't even noticeable at all. The response time is insane for a wireless mouse, and it surprised me a lot. I don't have a lot to say about the battery life yet, as this is my first day using it. I will say though, I charged the mouse to 68%, used it for an hour in Fortnite, and the battery was only 67% afterwards.

Here are the few cons I can think of:

reviews.review_title: Most satisfying mouse I have ever used; full stop.
reviews.review_description:
As someone who loves the Superlight and has been jamming out with version 2 of it along with a Logitech Pro X TKL paired with it, it's been nice to swap back to my Black Widow V4 along with the Viper Pro 3.

Right out of the box, and I am someone with medium to large hands, this mouse is just a pure delight to hold; it's not often I can say that my hands feel like they disappear when using a peripheral, but this mouse and the Superlight from Logi are the two mice that achieve that for me. Razer knew what they were doing here and it shows in the product; this will be my go-to mouse and I will alternate my Razer setup back to the Logitech set up as the mood strikes me to change things up week by week.

When it comes time for the Wooting 80HE to arrive, I will most likely be pairing the Viper Pro 3 with that board due to just how consistently good it feels; I am 3 hours deep into a play session and the battery is down to 98% and I'm using the 4K polling rate; not going to bother with 8K just yet.

It's hard to put into words here just how good the slight ergo shape of this mouse feels; I really have tried a number of different mice and this could be "the one"; I don't say this in a hyperbolic fashion either. It's rare that you use a gaming device where you just forget what you're using because it seamlessly blends into the play session.

For anyone looking to try this out, the asking price is steep. For a low frills mouse in the aesthetic department it really isn't going to be winning wards for it's design change to be not as sharp as it's predecessor. I for one really dig the smoother design and the light hump towards the back of the mouse, the finger ridges, or whatever you want to call them, on the L + R mouse clicks, all come together to suit whatever combination of grip you want to employ here. I am using a light palm grip and find that going claw and then relaxing my fingers feel natural.

The side buttons deserve a special award here; they are separated ever so slightly and their clicks are immediate / responsive. Truly the only gripe I have with my Superlight are the side buttons; Logitech really needs to take the oatmeal mush out of those and it will be a near perfect mouse for me.

Really curious to see what kind of competition this will spur with other manufacturers; that said, and for now, this is the best of the best for something that is here, on Amazon, that you can order and have by tomorrow while it's in stock. To whoever nabs one, enjoy; curious to see other reviews pop up on here.

reviews.review_title: Razer is back on top! Naga V2 is awesome.
reviews.review_description:
I used to despise Razer, but nowadays, the MMO mouse from Razer is pretty decent hardware. Their biggest problem has always been their software, however, and I must admit their support for software integrations is lacking. There's no OBS integration and no Discord integration. I'm getting by without setting up macros for hotkey combos by simply using my Logitech keyboard's macro keys for the integrations I want, and the only reason I didn't get another Logitech mouse was Logitech didn't make a new mouse model and discontinued their old, wired G600 model, making it cost too much to replace. I went with the Razer Naga V2 because it was somewhat cheap by comparison and wireless and I felt like giving other brands a try. I ended up really loving the build quality of the Naga V2, but Razer's software was still pretty terrible.

The hardware design is pretty good, but there are some ergonomics issues. The top left mouse click buttons (not left click) are hard to find by feel and also a little difficult to reach. There's no palm rest for a big hand to rest on. I think this mouse could benefit greatly from a 3d printable palm extension, but that would increase its weight, and the mouse is very lightweight. I ended up using a wrist rest that helped a little with mouse fatigue.

The battery is somewhat easy to swap out, and you don't have to swap often. It uses a single AA battery, and I opted to use a rechargeable lithium battery in it that adds some extra capacity.

The LEDs on the buttons are very dim by comparison to my other MMO mice, and they don't have the same flair I get from some other brands. The colors are customizable, but there's no wave effect on the mouse, which is weird because Razer's keyboards have the wave effect.

DPI is easy to change on-the-fly. I see no noticeable lag from being wireless. I also don't see any connectivity issues as long as I keep the mouse within 8 feet of its dongle.

Let me start by saying that this mouse is not a bad mouse in general, but if you are a gamer and you are here because you are looking for a replacement for your Logitech G600, you will probably not love this mouse.

I have been a G600 user for many years, and my last one recently started having some issues that made finding a replacement necessary. The V2 is *slightly* smaller overall than the G600, so it may not feel as good in your hand. It does have a bit of a lip on the right side where your ring finger rests, similar to the G600's shift button, so it seems like Razer could have implemented this feature, but did not.

The scroll wheel on top seems sluggish to me, in that it takes quite a few scrolls to move down a page, and I have not found any setting in the Razer Synapse app to change this. There is a button underneath the scroll wheel that "unlocks" the wheel and allows the wheel to spin freely instead of "clicking," however that is all this button does, it is not a functional button like the G7 and G8 buttons on the G600.

The V2 has two buttons in the top left corner of the left mouse button. By default these buttons are for turning the DPI up or down "on the fly," a feature which I have found to be entirely useless. I have never met anyone who adjusted their DPI once they found one they liked, much less needed to constantly change it. Even if you did need or want to do this, the buttons are pretty far away and not very easy to hit. You can re-map these buttons in the Synapse app, but again I have found they are too hard to reach for them to be useful.

By far the worst feature is the 12 side buttons. It has the same number of side buttons as the G600, however they are considerably smaller than the buttons on the G600. The buttons on the V2 are also not as beveled as the ones on the G600, are placed closer together, and do not have the home row "nubs" on the middle buttons which help you know where your thumb is. Additionally, where the G600 buttons are angled towards each other, with row 1 and 2 angled down towards each other, and rows 3 and 4 angled towards each other, the angling on the V2 side buttons is kind of all over the place, making it more difficult to move seamlessly from button to button.

As far as connectivity goes, I had no problem using the dongle to connect using the 2.4ghz option, and so far the mouse seems to track well. You will need to download the Razer Synapse app to customize keys and DPI settings. It does not seem to allow you to customize the polling rate, other than to choose from 125, 500 or 1000.

All things totaled, this mouse does not stack up for me and I will probably be returning it. I find that not having the G7 and G8 buttons on top, and all of the shortcomings with the side buttons make this very difficult to use while gaming. I find myself having to pay far too much attention to what my thumb is doing and trying to find the right buttons.

TL;DR - If you are a gamer, especially one who is accustomed to the G600, this mouse will disappoint you.

reviews.review_title: Swappable buttons, surprisingly capable and quality for price point, good middle ground for size
reviews.review_description:
This SOLAKAKA SM809 Pro has a lot of functionality for a budget $55 gaming mouse. The big feature is the number of programmable controls, so it makes the most sense for gamers, people who use a lot of macros, or power users who want shortcuts immediately available under their thumb. The PAW3311 sensor is premium, especially for this pricepoint. It provides accuracy and responsive in normal use, and the adjustable polling and DPI settings give it plenty of flexibility for gaming.

This mouse isn’t one that is completely ready to go when you get it. It really needs some configuration before it feels right or do what you want it to do. With 16 programmable buttons, the default setup is ok, but likely won’t do everything you want it to do, especially for specific games or functions. Fortunately, SOLAKAKA did something smart with the interchangeable magnetic side panels. If you do not need a full grid of thumb buttons, you can swap to a more traditional layout. The panels are easy to remove and reinstall, and that makes the mouse much more adaptable than a fixed MMO-style design. If you aren’t used to this type of mouse, you will find yourself accidentally hitting buttons, so it takes some time with it before it’s second nature.

Configuration is handled through SOLAKAKA's browser-based driver interface rather than requiring a traditional software installation. This provides more compatibility between OS and browser types. From there adjusting DPI, button assignments, macros, and the RGB effects if fairly intuitive. Once configured, the settings can be stored on the mouse, so you don’t have to reprogram it every time you move between computers.

Despite the obvious gaming appearance, I actually find the mouse to be comfortable for regular desktop use. The right-handed ergonomic shape fits my hand well, the scroll wheel is smooth, and the lightweight shell keeps it from feeling cumbersome during longer sessions. I feel like the size is a good middle ground for both larger and smaller hands, but it’s not unusable towards either group. The RGB lighting definitely gives it a gaming look, but it is configurable if you prefer something less flashy.

Connectivity is another strong point. It supports 2.4 GHz wireless, Bluetooth 5.0, and USB-C wired operation, so I can move it between computers without much hassle. The dongle is stored under a compartment on the bottom of the mouse, so you don’t have to worry about losing it when not in use. The included braided cable is also a nice quality touch and allows the mouse to be used while charging.

At around $55, the value makes sense primarily due to the swappable controls and programmable features. Even basic budget gaming mice often run double, so this price point is surprising for this level of capability and quality. However, someone who only needs a basic mouse would probably never use most of what it offers, but gamers and productivity users who regularly use macros can get a lot out of it. The ability to turn it from a button-heavy MMO mouse into a more conventional everyday mouse is what makes the SM809 Pro more useful than I initially expected.

reviews.review_title: I don't know how I ever lived without it.
reviews.review_description:
I'm very happy with this device. My laptop doesn't have an ethernet port and only has one USB-C SuperSpeed port, so I bought an ethernet to USB-C cable to connect my ethernet switch to the Anker and into my laptop's USB-C port, and it works great. I don't need a fast internet connection for the things I do, so my service is only a 50mbps symmetrical up/down connection, and that's what I get even while transferring files from my external between other devices, charging my phone, and using composite devices.

I bought the Anker 100W Compact and Foldable USB C Charger for it and it charges my S24 extremely fast.

It's very well built, yet super lightweight. I love the sleek, slender design. It's the perfect size to easily slide into a pocket, store in a desk drawer, or keep handy in a laptop case or backpack.

Using it is easy. Just plug it into your computer and plug your devices into it. Just make sure you have a power supply for it if you're charging or powering other devices, using external storage, or running anything else that taxes USB power.

I have had ZERO connectivity issues with it — no random disconnect/reconnect blips, no failed transfers for huge amounts of data that have taken up to 45 minutes, no static his or crackle when my headset is running through it... no problems at all. It's actually kind of spooky now that I think about it... I can't recall a time I've ever had a similar device that didn't have some nuance that got under my skin, like a loose connection, random disconnections, having to reinstall the drivers all the time, or having to troubleshoot just to get it connected for the first time.

The most stress I've put it through was with my keyboard connected, ethernet running through it, my S24 charging and transferring about ~20gb of pictures and videos to my 2T external HD at the same time that my laptop was transferring about ~500gb of media and documents to the HD, too, and I was surprised by how warm it DIDN'T get.

My only complaint is trivial and unique to my situation — I wish output cord was longer. About six inches would do. My laptop sits up on an adjustable stand that clamps to my desk, and the end where the output cord is hangs a few inches off of my desk. This puts extra stress on the USB-C port and can wear it out faster or damage it.

I haven't had a use for the HDMI port yet, but I eventually will. I use all of the other ports for my work and personal devices, though. These include: a 2tb external hard drive; a Poly Blackwire 3320 Series headset; a dongle for a wireless mouse/keyboard combo or a wired keyboard and a dongle for a wireless mouse; my Galaxy S24 charges and transfers files through it super fast; I have several thumb drives ranging from 20gb to 512gb that I regularly use; I recently bought an RCA/S Video-to-USB converter to digitize old home movies I plug into it, too.

reviews.review_title: A hub is not a dock. This is a very good USB-C hub
reviews.review_description:
Does what a hub ought to do - which is to say, you can plug it into one USB-C port and it will make power and data connectivity available to four downstream USB-C devices. The big caveats are that the host cable is extremely short and the power made available to downstream devices is significantly reduced from what the host provides. It's still a five star device because these short cables are universally present on all USB-C hubs, and the power limitations are less severe than other similar products that I have tested. Most importantly, the data connectivity offered by this unit is excellent, and it's extremely portable, being barely larger than the connectors it contains.

I would still very much prefer a version of this device with a USB-C female connector on the back instead of the permanently attached short cable but apparently there are valid technical reasons that USB-C hubs are not made in this way. Devices that offer more power and better cabling options are now classified as docks rather than hubs, they tend to be based on Thunderbolt rather than plain old USB-C, and some of these docks are quite excellent, but they are comparatively very expensive. This particular device is just a hub, it is very affordable compared to a dock, and it's as good as USB-C hubs get.

I will give the manufacturer points for build quality, the hub seems to built well and using quality materials. Unfortunately, that's about where the positive news ends and as far as usability goes I cannot recommend this device. I've listed below the problems I experienced within the first 24 hours of usage:

1) The switches outright just do not work for many devices. I tried several devices which seem to somehow just "ignore" the switch being turned off. I put ignore in quotes, because the device should not be built in a way that would allow any attached device to communicate with the host while it's off. For some devices, the switch does work correctly. However, for other devices, I can plug a USB cable into the hub and have it persistently connected to the host no matter how many times I toggle the switch on and off. This is a key indicator that the device was not designed in a secure way. When the toggle switch is off, power and connectivity should be completely disconnected to the port. The fact that I am able to bypass the toggle switch is an indicator that some sort of firmware workaround is being used. Bad news here.

2) Power delivery does not seem to work correctly on the hub. I'm using the power adapter that was delivered with the device which is plugged into a stable power source. Some devices which require power delivery (USB-PD) get stuck in an initializing state when drawing power from the hub. They get enough power to appear powered on, but the device never initializes and the host system can detect something was plugged in but cannot interface with the device. When I switch these devices to a different hub (or directly to the host), the issue is not present and the device works as expected.

3) Even devices that do connect, seem to have issues with performance and/or connectivity. When some devices are attached to the hub, the host operating system seems to hang while the device is connecting. I experience this on about 1/3 of my attempts with any mass storage device, and some devices fairly consistently. When I do get a device to connect to the host, my transfer speeds are considerably lower than if I had used a different hub or connected directly to the host.

All in all, I absolutely do not recommend this device. There are several clear indicators of poor and unsafe design when it comes to this hub, and I would not trust that it delivers power cleanly or that there's any consistent integrity on file transfers.

Again, all of these issues were experienced within the first 24 hours of usage. I tested over a dozen different devices with this hub, of varying types and manufacturer. If I had this many issues straight away, I can guarantee it's not an isolated incident. Even if my hub was "defective", there's no way it would have been defective in a way that would selectively allow some devices to connect while toggled off.

Let this be a warning to you!

reviews.review_title: Great 10gbps USB-C Hub, worked with Anker support through compat issues with PD4 iteration 1
reviews.review_description:
Original Review (updates below):

-----

The moment I noticed this thing on Amazon, I bought it and it literally just arrived. Finally, 4K60 over just USB-C with other ports (including making up to 10Gbps available to them) for a reasonable price. Unfortunately, the first two things I've done with it were both disappointing. I'll cut to the chase, the power delivery pass through isn't working with one of their own chargers.

The first device I tried connecting this with is my Anker PD4 with one USB-C cable as the only thing plugged into it so I can test the truly up to 100W (-15 for its own power) claims. I've tried connecting it with Apple's 2m USB-C charge cable (100w capable) and an equivalent CableMatters cable that also supports 100W. When plugged directly into my laptop, both of these cables immediately start charging it and show up as 100W power sources. When this Anker hub is plugged in and either of them is connected to the power delivery port on the side of it, the laptop does not charge (laptop is a 16" Macbook Pro, I've tried multiple ports just for the heck of it).

My second complaint is that when absolutely nothing is plugged into it, it becomes fairly warm to the touch. Why, when it's doing nothing, is it hot? I'm clearly not running data or even power through it so I have low hopes for it under load.

The fact that it doesn't work in exactly the scenario they want it to most (a MacBook Pro with one of their own chargers) seems like a pretty big fail. I've got lots of USB-C things though so I thought I'd grab a couple and try those. Using an Apple 96W USB-C charger, the device does pass through power delivery properly. It shows up as providing 79W to the laptop (siphoning off 17W in this instance). I also have a 56W Aukey charger that splits power between a USB-A port and a USB-C port that can provide 45W of power delivery. When plugged into that charger it does appear to work as well and appears in macOS as a 30W power source.

Maybe the problem is the Anker PD4? But it works fine providing power to the laptop directly. Would love to hear from Anker about these two products working together and what I should actually expect. Having it be unreliable for power delivery isn't great, but power and heat aside (it is getting a little bit warmer now that it's providing power from the Apple power adapter, but still definitely holdable), the hardware looks and feels good and the cable feels durable. Worth also noting that there's a white LED ring on the side of it that appears to be always on when it's plugged in. Don't know why it needs an LED.

-----

Update, June 22, 2020:

I've done some more testing and Anker has reached out to me to investigate what might be the issue. I can say that the hub works as I would expect from a quick test with my iPad Pro 11" with the above functioning chargers. It was able to pass through power with the 96W Apple Charger on the other end to both the iPad port as well as a Magic Keyboard port. The ethernet adapter showed up in iOS settings and an external drive was functional. When connected via the Magic Keyboard, which is a power only connection, as expected it provided only power.

Still no power passthrough of any kind when connected to the PD4.

-----

Update July 1, 2020:

I've written back and forth with Anker and they've sent me a replacement hub. It also doesn't work with the PD4. I've tried multiple USB-C cables but they have also shipped a cable to test with it. For now I'm increasing the review from 2 to 3 stars because I am more and more suspicious about the PD4 and less about this hub. They claim that they have tested the setup I have separately without issue, and I've sent video showing the problems I've encountered, so the troubleshooting is ongoing.

Have had a chance to use Ethernet on it without issue. Still need to try to test out its throughput when trying to use a 10Gbps USB-C enclosure and a 4K60 monitor at the same time (+ ethernet).

More updates to come.

-----

Update July 10, 2020:

I've continued to talk with Anker support and they shipped me a replacement PD4. The one I had was labeled as "Iteration 1" on its barcode, the one I got back was labeled "Iteration 2". I tested it out and it works perfectly with this hub, passing through the correct amount of power to multiple Macbook Pros and fast charging an iPad Pro. Clearly the fault doesn't lie with this hub and is instead an issue with the first iteration PD4, so I'm updating my review accordingly. Working with Anker support was great.

I've also been able to test USB-C throughput (without driving a display as well so far) and it properly utilizes 10Gbps. I've attached some extra images showing various devices connected to it (keyboard dongle, SD card, USB-C 10Gbps external SSD enclosure, USB sound card, ethernet).

reviews.review_title: Like It, but it required additional equipment to charge iPad Air 4
reviews.review_description:
I am exploring ways to make my iPad behave like a laptop, and with this little device, I am on my way. One of my primary concerns is that sometimes I have to troubleshoot routers at other people's homes. So I tried it out on my home. I found that I had to install an app from the manufacturer to make it work, then I had to reboot the router. Then, I got an amazing interface that was not the same as the interface on my laptop. It told me that I need a firmware update, but at this point, I am more comfortable doing the update on my laptop. One quirk I don't understand is that I plugged the PD port into my power cube, and the iPad told me it wasn't charging. That isn't good. I might have to return it and shop for a different brand. The newer Apple devices are awfully picky as to where they get their power from.

Update: I found the email for Anker customer support, sent an email, and they got right back to me. Here is what they said:

"Please first know: Due to the power input limitations of mobile devices, this hub can not provide pass-through charging to tablets (including iPad Pro/Air) or phones when using the original wall charger that came with your mobile device. To support full-speed charging for iPad Pro/Air, use an adapter that supports at least 15V (45W)."

I found that the 3 foot power cord that Apple sent me is nowhere near long enough for charging while using the dock, so I sent away for a 45W charger and a 10 foot USB-C to USB-C charging cable that was compatible with iPad. Please be aware that Apple has circuitry embedded in the cord and you cannot use just any cord. The equipment I got was this:

Charger https://smile.amazon.com/gp/product/B083BRKMJQ/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_asin_title_o00_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1

Cord https://smile.amazon.com/gp/product/B07LF1FNRV/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_asin_title_o00_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1

Cords are not rated in either volts or watts, so I sent another email to Anker asking if a 3 amp cable would work, and they told me that it should. Pay attention to the amperage when purchasing a cable to go with a high wattage charger.

The cord that I purchased also comes in a 15 foot length. If this rig works, I will also purchase the 15 foot cord. The reason being that sometimes I need to do stuff in other people's houses, and I cannot count on a nearby outlet.

I will update when the new equipment comes.

Update: I installed a 45W charger with a USB-C TO USB-C cable that was advertised for iPads, and now my iPad is charging through the PD port, so that problem is taken care of.

I sold the iPad and bought a 2019 MacBook Pro. The MacBook Pro has four Type C USB ports only, no others. I use one of the ports on the Mac for charging and another for the hub. I use the Type 3 USB ports on the hub for my mouse and graphic tablet. I like wired mice, because they use a wire for power, are more reliable, and do not generate dead batteries to pollute the environment. I wish the hub had an additional Type 2 or 3 USB port. Maybe I will buy an additional adapter, because I can't find a hub that sports the extra ports. I looked for a mouse that would plug into a USB C port, but did not find one to my taste. I like wired keyboards for the same reason I like wired mice.

At any rate, all these wires that will not plug directly into my computer makes kind of a clutter, as depicted in my photo. Not much I can do about it at this stage of the game, however.

Allows multiple devices (ext drives, keyboard) and Ethernet and HMDI cables to be plugged into one USB computer port (also has two card slots, SD and microSD)

When I want to take my laptop somewhere (which is, after all, the whole point of a laptop!), I only need to unplug one thing. (Although I do have to remember to eject the external drives or I get a nagging reminder from the OS).

I bought this a while back and while shopping for a second dock for my wife, I came across a lot of reviews where people are complaining about this thing. I relate to those experiences, but the problem is not the dock itself. Mine worked at first and then it started to work intermittently. Sometimes, my external monitor would come on and sometimes it wouldn't. I tried it with different Anker cables (I had been using the one that came with it) and I even tried it with different Macbooks. At one point, I actually thought the problem was probably with Apple. It was really frustrating and annoying. But then I decided to try a new Thunderbolt 4 cable I had purchased from Cable Matters. I didn't really expect that to make a difference, but it solved everything. It has worked perfectly for over a year now. I connect my laptop and I can instantly use my monitor and get to work without a hassle. I've since realized that while Anker makes good power bricks and even hubs, they make really crappy cables. I have a LOT of them, unfortunately. They short out very quickly and I've noticed they often separate near the connectors. For stuff like lightning cables, you know right away when it stops working. But Thunderbolt cables can be confusing because they don't just fail. A bad cable will work really well sometimes and then not at all other times. It doesn't make sense that you would get perfect resolution on your monitor one day and not even be able to get it to turn on the next. For high bandwidth like 4K external monitors, you really just need a high quality, reliable cable. Don't try to save money on that and don't buy cables from Anker. I hope this is helpful to people.

reviews.review_title: The Travel Dock in My Laptop Bag
reviews.review_description:
What I like

Plug-and-play. One USB-C cable in, several ports out. No drivers, no setup, no configuration.

HDMI output for plugging into a hotel-room TV or conference projector without an adapter.

SD card reader for moving photos off a camera. The microSD reader is a bonus.

Two USB-A ports are enough for a mouse, a USB stick, or a card reader I already own.

85 W pass-through charging means I can keep my laptop charged through the hub when I have a USB-C charger handy.

Lives in the laptop bag and is ready when I travel. It is the kind of accessory that pays for itself the first time you really need it.

Compact and light. I forget it is in the bag until I need it.

What annoys me

Not a daily driver on my home desk. My home computers already have the ports I need, so the hub sits in the bag most of the time.

Bus-powered. No battery, no separate power input. I am not trying to power a hungry external device through it, so this is fine, but it is not a “real docking station” with its own power supply.

One HDMI output. If I wanted to drive two external monitors, I would need a different hub or a dock with display-multiplication support. The transcript says “second HDMI port,” and this hub gives me one, not two.

No Ethernet port. Wireless works almost everywhere I travel, but a wired Ethernet jack would be a real bonus on hotel networks that block Wi-Fi or charge for it.

I do not actually use it on my Mac mini. It would work, but I have not built the habit of plugging the mini through the hub. That is a me problem, not an Anker problem.

Who it is for, and who should skip it

If you travel with a laptop and need HDMI, an SD card reader, extra USB-A, and the option to charge the laptop through a single cable, this is the right tool. It is small enough to leave in the bag and useful enough to justify its weight.

Skip it if you want a full desktop dock with its own power supply, multiple display outputs, Ethernet, and the ability to drive a multi-monitor workstation. That is a different product class, and a single USB-C hub with bus power will not do that job.

Skip it if your laptop already has every port you need. The hub is solving a missing-port problem, and if you do not have one, it will just sit in your bag.

Verdict

The Anker USB-C 7-in-1 hub is a small, useful travel accessory that lives in my laptop bag and earns its place every time I take a trip. It is not exciting. It is not a daily driver. It is the kind of thing that disappears into your workflow and then you are grateful for it when you need it.

Grade: A—if you want a single-cable travel dock for a laptop or Mac mini. Buy the linked listing if your use case matches mine.

reviews.review_title: Misleading Power Claims and Poor Multi-Device Performance
reviews.review_description:
Misleading Power Claims and Poor Multi-Device Performance

I purchased this charging station because it advertises up to 140W charging and supports multiple devices. Unfortunately, it only delivers the advertised power when a single USB-C device is connected.

The moment I connect a second USB-C cable, the power output drops dramatically. For example, a port that was delivering around 100W drops to about 7W, and a 140W output falls to roughly 35W. This makes it practically unusable for charging multiple high-power devices at the same time.

The biggest issue is that the product is marketed as a 10-port charging station, which implies that multiple devices can be charged efficiently in parallel. Instead, the charger appears to aggressively redistribute power whenever another device is plugged in, causing charging speeds to become extremely slow. If you're charging a laptop and then connect a phone or tablet, expect the laptop charging speed to drop significantly.

Went on a big family trip recently, and between us we had like 6 or 7 different chargers and cords for our tablets, phones, wearables, earbuds etc. I came back from that trip and figured I needed to get a charging station to cut down on all the plugs. I particularly wanted to get one with the old USB A plugs in it, since we had older devices and cords. This one fit the bill perfectly.

reviews.review_description:
I honestly didn’t expect to like this keyboard this much. I upgraded from a Razer BlackWidow V3, and the difference is immediately noticeable.

The magnetic switches feel incredibly smooth and responsive, and being able to adjust the actuation point and use Rapid Trigger is a game changer for competitive gaming. Movement feels much more precise, especially in Fortnite. The keyboard also feels extremely well built and premium.

What I really like is that it isn’t only great for gaming. For everyday use, studying, and programming, I can switch to a normal profile and it feels just as good to type on.

reviews.review_title: Incredible for coding, even better for gaming,
reviews.review_description:
This one gets reviewed from two angles. As a professional software engineer I live by the quality of my keyboard and have been opinionated about keyboards for more than 20 years, so I ran this as my daily driver for a week to test it out. It was quiet, consistent, and responsive. Despite the gaming branding, this is probably the best tenkeyless keyboard I've ever typed on. Turn the lighting off and it can be dropped onto any office desk without getting a second glance. The high quality PBT keycaps have a texture that doesn't go slick and greasy, and they shouldn't shine up the way ABS does after a few months of heavy use. The switches are factory lubed with a dense foam layer underneath, so there's no hollow plastic rattle and no metallic ping. It's also not the clicking like you get from mechanical switches. It's a low, dull sound that doesn't get annoying in a quiet room or on a call. The adjustable actuation mattered more than I expected for office use. Setting it deeper than a gamer would means you stop firing off accidental characters when your fingers graze the home row, which is something that makes most fast-actuation boards frustrating for long-form writing and code. The aluminum top gives it a solid build, so it doesn't flex or walk across the desk, and the detachable USB-C cable means a longer lifespan.

After my week ended I handed it to my teenage son, the gamer, and I really don't think I'm getting it back. He found things I never would have. Rapid Trigger resets the key the instant it starts to rise instead of waiting for a fixed point, which he says completely changes counter-strafing. Snap Tap prioritizes whichever direction key you pressed most recently, so pressing A while holding D doesn't leave you standing there. Dynamic Keystroke lets a single key fire up to four different actions depending on how far down you press it, and Snap Flex assigns one action on press and a different one on release. He set up a key that peeks a corner on a light press and pulls back on release. I didn't even know keyboards did that, but he's raving about it. The 8000Hz polling means it reports to the PC eight times more often than a standard board. He swears he can feel it. I'm skeptical it's perceptible, but he's the one winning matches. All of the tuning lives in the browser based software, which allows you to adjust lighting, actuation and keybinds without installing anything.

I really only had two very minor complaints about this keyboard. The switches aren't hot-swappable. Every switch fails eventually, even fancy magnetic switches rated at millions of actuations, and at this price it's disappointing that there's no path to replacing one when it does. The other is the calibration routine that needs to be run every time it's installed or keycaps are replaced, because that part of the software is just tedious and could be better designed. Those are very minor gripes against everything else here.

This is a fantastic keyboard, and I'd recommend it without hesitation. Whether you're a professional keyboarder and are looking for a great tenkeyless for daily use, or a gamer looking for an edge, you really can't go wrong with this thing.

reviews.review_title: Maybe im ready to give Razer another chance
reviews.review_description:
The Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Mini keyboard is the latest addition to their Hall Effect Magnetic keyboard lineup. If you haven't been keeping up with keyboard technologies, compared to traditional keyboard switches made by companies like Cherry, they are now utilizing magnets and lasers to create a much more responsive key press reducing latency and allowing for customizable key actuation based on the users preference. I am a hobbyist with keyboard tech, where I have built a good variety of keyboards with DIY kits, customized some of my own, and tend to go out of my way to try new technologies. This is my third time trying a Hall Effect keyboard, with my first being the Steelseries Apex Pro ( with HyperMagnetic switches) and the original Razer Huntsman.

I didn't hold onto either of those keyboards very long as at the time they were very expensive compared to their traditional counterparts. They also didn't wow me out of the box with their switch technology. Keypresses felt weak, as if there was no feedback to register that I had hit a key. It also took a lot of tweaking to get them to what I would consider a usable state with accurate typing. Which leaves me with the new Razer Huntsman, where I am happy to report it doesn't share any of these problems.

The recent revisions have made many changes, improving the texture on the keycaps, the sound of the keypresses, the out of box actuation is exactly what I want, and the 8khz polling is probably helping with how responsive the keys feel. I generally use full size keyboards as I like to have a numpad, but the feel of this keyboard is winning me over to make it my daily driver away from my Mountain Everest Max with Cherry Blues. Lubed Holy Panda switches are the only ones I own that might feel a little bit better than these, but the overall responsiveness of these HE Magentics is something I haven't had the pleasure of experiencing before.

My closing statement will be that I started my PC peripheral journey with Razer back when they released the first Blackwidow keyboard & OG Razer Naga. I have watched their products go through sharp declines, and had a time of regret after recommending them to several friends and watching their mice break down on them within a year each. I am hesitant to recommend them again due to the many issues I have had across a few years before ultimately moving away from their products entirely. I will update this review if I encounter any issues with the keyboard as I daily drive it.

Post note: I forgot to mention Synapse in this review, as I don't really want to use it. I will add it in if I change my mind but luckily the keyboard works fine without it. Windows Dynamic Lighting isn't working with the keyboard out of the box but I know of other 3rd party software that used to work with Razer that I preferred. After one pop up the Razer software installer hasn't appeared again which is nice.

reviews.review_title: Razer’s Hall Effect Switches Are a Major Improvement
reviews.review_description:
Razer has made adjustable-actuation keyboards before, but its previous analog Huntsman models relied on optical switches. This is its first real move into the Hall effect keyboard space, and the switch change is not just a spec-sheet distinction. These new magnetic switches feel noticeably smoother and less scratchy than the optical analog switches I have used in the past, especially when pressing a key slowly or typing for longer periods.

They also retain a full 4.0mm range of travel, which is less common than I expected among Hall effect gaming keyboards. I can set a very shallow actuation point for movement keys in competitive games without making the entire board feel like a hair trigger. For typing, I prefer a deeper actuation and the full key travel because it feels more natural and gives me fewer accidental inputs. That flexibility makes the Huntsman V3 HE easier to live with as an everyday keyboard rather than something designed exclusively for ranked matches.

Rapid trigger works as expected, resetting each key based on movement rather than waiting for it to return to a fixed reset point. In shooters, directional inputs feel crisp and immediate, particularly when rapidly stopping, strafing, or changing direction. Snap Tap can prioritize the newest input between two movement keys, while Snap Flex adds another way to activate commands based on releasing a key. These features will matter most to serious FPS players, but the adjustable actuation is useful even outside competitive gaming.

The 8000Hz polling rate gives the keyboard plenty of performance headroom. I cannot pretend the jump from an already fast gaming keyboard is transformative in every game, but inputs feel consistently immediate, and there is no sense that the keyboard is holding anything back. It is also possible to store multiple profiles, which is useful when I want aggressive gaming settings without using those same settings while typing or programming.

I generally like the 65% layout because it leaves much more space for the mouse while retaining dedicated arrow keys. It is compact enough for an FPS setup without feeling as restrictive as a 60% board, although anyone who regularly uses the function row, navigation cluster, or numpad should expect a period of adjustment. The secondary functions are manageable, but they are still secondary functions.

Build quality is appropriately solid for the price. The aluminum top case gives the board a sturdy feel, the doubleshot PBT keycaps have a pleasant texture, and the detachable USB-C cable makes it easier to pack or replace the cable later. The switches sound and feel much more refined than Razer’s earlier analog optical boards, though this is still a gaming keyboard rather than a heavily dampened custom mechanical board.

At $120, this is competitively priced for a Hall effect keyboard from a major gaming brand, especially with 8000Hz polling, rapid trigger, adjustable actuation, onboard profiles, and a full 4.0mm travel range. The real improvement for me is not one headline feature but how much better these magnetic switches feel. They are fast enough for competitive play, smooth enough to enjoy, and versatile enough that I can type on the keyboard all day without wishing I had switched back to a conventional mechanical board.
